coachMessages.text: These four discs look like the letter J. Before reading on — where do you think the winning move goes?

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show a mid-game position (8–12 moves played) where Gray has exactly four discs arranged in a J shape: a vertical pair forming the lower stem, one disc extending horizontally right at the top of the stem (the hook top), and one disc on the diagonal rising from the stem base. The J anchor disc (bottom of the stem) should be at an odd-indexed row (0-indexed: row 1, 3, or 5). Mark the four Gray J-shape discs with 'win' overlays. Do not mark the threat cells yet — let the student look first. Legend: 'win' = The four J-shape discs.</board instructions>

Four Gray discs arranged in a J shape. The stem of the J is vertical, the hook extends horizontally, and the diagonal arm rises from the base. Before the next slide reveals the threats, study the shape: where would Gray's winning move(s) complete a four-in-a-row?

coachMessages.text: Two threats converge on the same column. Playing in that column creates a fork — one move, two wins.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show the same J-shape position as slide 1. Now reveal the two primary threats: (1) the horizontal arm of the J extended one cell to the right (or left, depending on orientation) — a horizontal major threat; (2) the diagonal arm extended one cell — a diagonal major threat. Both threat cells should converge on the same column (the shared column where both lines can be completed). Mark both threat cells with 'tg' overlays. Also mark the four J-shape discs with 'win' overlays to show which discs form each line. Legend: 'win' = J-shape pattern discs, 'tg' = Both threat cells (both in the same column — fork).</board instructions>

The J-shape creates two threats that converge on the same column: one horizontal, one diagonal. Playing in that column sets up a fork — both threats become live simultaneously. Your opponent faces two winning lines in one move and can only block one. This is why the J-shape is so powerful: the setup move forces a no-win situation.

coachMessages.text: Your opponent blocks one arm of the J. The other arm is still alive. Try blocking the horizontal — the diagonal survives.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show the same J-shape position as slide 1–2, but now show the result AFTER the opponent makes the most natural block: filling the horizontal arm's completing cell. Mark the opponent's blocking disc with 'td' ('Blocks horizontal threat'). The diagonal threat cell should still be marked 'tg' ('Diagonal still alive'). Make it visually clear that blocking one arm leaves the other completely open. Legend: 'td' = Opponent blocks horizontal arm, 'tg' = Diagonal threat survives (Gray wins next move).</board instructions>

Whatever your opponent blocks, the other arm of the J survives. Block the horizontal threat cell — the diagonal is still alive. Block the diagonal threat cell — the horizontal is still alive. Your opponent would need two moves to handle both, but they only get one. The J-shape is won on the move that creates both threats simultaneously.

coachMessages.text: The J looks right — but the anchor is on an even row (0-indexed). Count the gap to the threat cell: it's even, so your opponent reaches it first.

slides.infoProse:
<board instructions>Show a position with a visually identical J-shape to slides 1–3 but where the anchor disc (bottom of the J stem) is at an even-indexed row (0-indexed: row 0, 2, or 4). Because the anchor is on an even row, the gap from the column's current height to the key threat cell will be even — Gray's opponent lands on it first. Mark the anchor disc with 'td' ('Even-row anchor — J does not work here') and the threat cell with 'td' as well ('Your opponent reaches this first'). Contrast this with a version showing an odd-row anchor where 'tg' marks the valid threat cell. Legend: 'td' = Even-row anchor (J is a ghost threat), 'tg' = Odd-row anchor (J is real — Gray owns the threat cell).</board instructions>

The J-shape only works when the anchor disc sits at an odd-indexed row (0-indexed: rows 1, 3, 5). This parity condition ensures that Gray, not the opponent, is the player who naturally lands on the key threat cells as those columns fill.

With an even-indexed anchor, the gap from the column top to the threat cell is even — the opponent reaches it first. The shape looks identical, but the J is a ghost. Always check the anchor row before committing to building a J.

socratic.goalPrompt: One of these J-shapes wins — the other is a ghost. Which column do you play to activate the real J?
socratic._boardInstructions: Show a mid-game position (14–18 moves played) where Yellow has two complete four-disc J-shaped clusters that look visually identical but differ only in their anchor row. One J has its anchor disc at an odd row (row 1 or 3, 0-indexed); its fork fires at col 2 — mark its four discs with 'tg' overlays and the col 2 target cell with 'tg' ('Play here — fork is live'). The other J has its anchor at an even row (row 0 or 2); mark its corresponding threat cell with 'td' ('Opponent reaches this first'). No other distractors; the only puzzle is identifying which anchor row is odd. Legend: 'tg' = Real J discs and fork column (col 2), 'td' = Ghost J threat cell (dead).

Spot the J-Shape pattern and play the key move to exploit it.
